title: The Tongue as the Beginning of Sin and Virtue
english: Not because 'righteousness has persecuted me' [Ps 22:19], but do not forsake me, do not become distant from me. God forsakes someone when they are worthy to suffer grievous things. I do not say this to mean that He tests them with grievous things; He is not not-forsaking, but when one, having grievous things, is defeated and cast down, then You do not forsake me, if You do not depart from me. I have clung to You; I have become one spirit toward You. When one clings to the Lord, and the Lord to him. 'My soul has clung to You behind You' [Ps 63:8].

Cry out for my help, O Lord of my salvation [Ps 27:7]. You stand away from me if I sin, not if I am hated unjustly, nor even if some magnify themselves against me. And You are Lord and God of my salvation. But salvation does not touch the flesh, nor is it found regarding external things, but regarding the soul itself. This is the said eternal salvation; for it 'became'—the Christ, clearly—'eternal salvation to all those obeying Him.' The flesh's 'eternal salvation', which doctors bring to it, or that which a pilot saves for those sailing, is not eternal; for these will soon die again. But the salvation of God is eternal; He is their salvation.

1–2 To the end, to Ithium. I said: I will guard my ways so as not to sin in my tongue. This is one of the Psalms. In Ezra and in the [Book of the] Remaining, there is a memory of each name of those being submitted. And this, then, is one of them, or perhaps he himself composed the psalm for David, or having received it from David, he proclaimed it. And it is the work of the Psalms to say their psalms, both those they themselves composed and those others arranged.

This, then, is a victory song. Often the sinner is troubled by these things, but after conquering and trampling him and taking him under hand, [the psalmist] sends back the song; for no one sings a victory song while still warring and being warred against, but in the having conquered. Likewise, Moses and all the Jewish multitude did not say a victory song when they were against Pharaoh, but when they saw him become a drowning man: 'Let us sing to the Lord, for gloriously He has been glorified; He has cast horse and rider into the sea' [Ex 15:1]. When the horse and its rider were cast into the sea, and Pharaoh's chariots and the power of the...

God cast the Red Sea into the sea, and then a victorious song was appropriately sent up. And David says in the seventy-first psalm: 'In the day when he rescued him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul, then he said: I will love you, O Lord my strength' (Ps 71:5), and all the rest which the song contains. It is a prayer before the war and in the war, but a victorious hymn and song after the destruction of the war, after capturing the enemies.

I said: 'I will guard my ways so as not to sin in my tongue' (Ps 34:13). For almost every practical sin has its beginning in the word. Regarding the young man whom the prostitute—who is personified in the proverbs, that is, being a woman or a false glory or a deception starting from words—is able to ensnare: for it is said, 'She led him astray with much intercourse' or enticement, and 'with the nooses through the lips she hollowed him out' (Prov 2:3/7). And behold, the word has become the beginning of sin. And the elders, indeed, those remaining according to Sophronius, started a word toward her.

If, therefore, someone does not sin in the tongue, he guards the ways well; for he said that the beginning of these ways is the word. And from the opposite of all good works, the word is the beginning. But he does not speak only about those ways; he added, 'so as not to sin in my tongue' (Ps 34:13). Yet sinning in the tongue is not the same as saying, 'My tongue will meditate on your righteousness' (Ps 119:9). 'The beginning of your words is truth' (Ps 119:160). The cause of saying your words is your truth; I will make this manifest if I know it. Therefore, upon the virtues and the well-flowing ways, truth is the beginning, the cause. But upon the forbidden ways, from which it is necessary to guard oneself and from which it is proper to turn away, the word is the beginning, as has already been said.

I set a guard upon my mouth (Ps 34:13). Remember how he said 'not to sin in the tongue': 'I set a guard upon my mouth.' Since 'from the words someone is justified and from his words he is condemned' (Matt 12:37), it is necessary for the mouth to place a guard, so that I may say the [good] things and not the [bad], that we may speak the profitable things and be silent about the harmful ones; for no one is able at once to bring forth words that both justify and condemn. Something like this is said with an enigma in the proverbs: 'Death and life are in the hand of the tongue' (Prov 18:21). And the 'hand' of the 'tongue' is the word.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Wisdom in Silence and the Renewal of Sorrow
english: The activity of the tongue. He who speaks what is beneficial and leads into the kingdom of life has life in the tongue. But he who speaks the opposite and the forbidden things has death in his own word called a 'tongue'. And in another scripture it says: 'With your words make a balance and a weight' (Prov 16:11). It is necessary to speak having weighed; it is necessary to have a balance and to cast the words upon each scale. And if the upright words are found to be balanced, it is proper to choose those and to proclaim them, but to turn away from the bad ones.

Again it is said: 'The lips of the wise are taught by perception' (Ps 51:13). When someone speaks having perceived, the lips are taught, not opening them to every word, but to what is beneficial. 'I will open my lips and my mouth shall proclaim your praise' (Ps 51:14). He who has the taught lips, having perceived that what he intends to speak is beneficial, opened them. But when they harm what is being uttered, he closes and binds the lips with perception; he binds the word.

'In the standing of the sinner against me, I was made deaf and humbled, and I kept silence for the sake of good things' (Ps 31:5). Often appearing, the sinner provokes and is called out to the things pleasing to him. If, therefore, he ever stands [against us], it is our part to make him stand; for if we do not give him a place, he is not able to stand. But to stand in this way is to stand in battle. It is necessary to be silent; for he often provokes; because the serpent, having stood against Eve, provoked her word and harmed her. It was necessary to be silent, having received perception of her own weakness or of the sin that had come before, not to speak anything to her, but to keep silence for the sake of good things.

And the 'keeping silence for the sake of good things' does not say 'not to speak the good things', but to have a silence made wise from the good things. For example, having taken up virtue, a prudent man knew that he must not respond out of the good, that is, out of prudence. I kept silence toward the standing revealed and provoking toward sin. If, therefore, that young man had been responding to nothing from right understanding toward the harlot, he would not have 'been led astray by much association' (1 Tim 5:15) nor 'been enticed by the morsels of his lips' (Prov 5:3). I kept silence, therefore, when the good things had come upon me, persuading me not to respond to him. He does not say: 'I kept silence so as not to speak the good things', but 'so as not to speak the provoking things'. And this silence has become to me from...

The wisdom of the good things which hinders such a conversation. "He is found wise while being silent." He who thus remains silent is found wise. And it is indeed wisdom to know to whom one must speak and to whom one must not, and when to bring forward words and when not. "He is therefore found wise while being silent, and he is silent, for he has no answer." And this man possesses a certain quietness of mind; for having known that he has no answer, he keeps peace. "And he is wise, being silent, knowing the right time." This man is perfect.

And "my sorrow was renewed" (Psalm 39:10). Then the sorrow is renewed when the sinner stands in reflection upon what he has done, upon which it is necessary to grieve. And just as the sorrow received a renewal, renewal is to dwell in a house at first. A renewal, therefore, is to lead that which has already withered and is silent into flowering. "My sorrow" therefore "was renewed." Having said, "I kept my ways not to sin with my tongue" (Psalm 119:11), I knew that I had sinned. Therefore "my sorrow was renewed." And it is blessed for one who has sinned to experience a renewal of sorrow and not of pleasure; for he who rejoices over what he has done and brings those things back into the midst again, renews [the sin]. But he who grieves, having perceived that it is necessary to guard the ways and not to sin with the tongue, renews the sorrow, weeping and grieving, "working the sorrow according to God, which is repentance." In this, he grieves entirely in the recognizing that it has entirely happened in such matters.

"My heart was warmed within me" (Psalm 39:3). One may say: my heart has received heat just as warmth, and from the renewal of sorrow. And one may also say this: because I seized myself intensely and I am being consumed and I weep aloud the sorrow, "my heart was warmed," it has become fiery. "In" indeed "my practice, a fire burned up" (Psalm 39:2), consuming and making me ash; for they were hay and wood and other things. I have this consuming fire not only in the being perfected, but also in my practicing the sorrow. And the "within me" is also good. The heart becomes hot so that the heat spreads even to the outside. Those, indeed, who are burning with passion do not have a heart warmed within, but, having spread to the outside, they have the state of one being pressed. It is as if it were said: "I was troubled and I did not speak."
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Number of Days and Enlightenments
english: Having experienced a disturbance in thought or in reasoning, and having done nothing according to that disturbance of thoughts, nor even having spoken, he possesses the state of having been disturbed and not having spoken. Such a person has within him a heart having been warmed. 'And in my meditation fire shall be kindled' (Ps 39:16). My inner self. And thus for each of us, two men have stood, the one outside, the other inside. Therefore, when a disturbance arises in the soul and does not transfer the disturbance to the outer man, but keeps it within so as to recognize it and weep over it, he has within him a heart having been warmed, not in order to act, but in order not to act. 'In my meditation the fire burns.' In others, by voice and by action and by thought, a fire burns, consuming them, burning them. 'Their heart was warmed like a fiery furnace.' Here the meditation is like a fire that has burned, having a combustible material lying beneath. And the meditation and the heat of the Holy [Spirit] is the all-consuming, which comes to pass by the blowing Spirit. Therefore the fire burns in order that it may act, not in order that it may harm and consume. 'Was not our heart burning within us while he opened to us the Scriptures?' (Lk 24:32). This burning is to be praised. And observe also regarding manufactured things: some are heated in order that they may be reshaped and become a vessel, gold or silver. But if wood or something else is set on fire, the heat is harmful.

'I spoke in a tongue.' Even if I did not let it become outward, but it remained within me, through a burning from meditation it made itself for me, and so I spoke in a tongue: 'Make known to me, Lord, my end' (Ps 62:5). From my own tongue I said this; for the tongue according to the nature of the possessor is this: for example, the temperate man, speaking the things of temperance, speaks in his own tongue, the tongue of the temperate man, not in the tongue of a human [deceiver]. And the one desiring to learn his own end and to offer his life to God, in my tongue, not in the tongue of a deceitful man, but I, desiring to know my end, spoke in a tongue. This my word is not a counterfeit. When a hypocrite speaks concerning temperance while not being temperate, he does not speak in his own tongue. But the temperate man, when he delivers discourses concerning temperance, speaks in the tongue of the temperate man. No hypocrite, therefore, speaks in the natural tongue, but in the counterfeit tongue. The wolf, when he [is...]

Begging like a sheep to enter Christ's flock, he speaks not in his own tongue, but imitates the voice of the sheep, so that, meeting like with like, he might harm. 'Make known to me, Lord, my end and the number of my days, what it is' (Psalm 39:10). Observe how the one saying this is a repentant person. 'Help me to guard my ways, to set a guard over my mouth' (Psalm 39:11-12). When the sinner stood against me and was provoking, I received good in my mind from the experience of not speaking to him.

This is therefore what I say; since I saw myself lacking much—for I had only just begun to progress—'Make known to me, Lord, my end,' so that I might know how much time of life remains to me, if it is sufficient for completion and fulfillment. Thus also another was saying: 'Declare to me the brevity of my days; do not bring me back in the midst of my days' (Psalm 39:13). In a certain way, I am in the midst of the days that come from the Holy Light. Do not then bring me back in such a way. Therefore, fulfill my days.

But God fulfills the days of some not by providing an increase of them; for when it is said, 'I will fill him with length of days' concerning the righteous, we do not say that he makes him many-years. There are also impious people who have lived many years. 'And the number of my days' (Psalm 39:10). It is also possible to say 'the number of my days' meaning: you have enlightened me much, I have become [composed of] days; for each enlightenment is a day. Therefore, reveal to me the number of my enlightenments, so that I might know what I lack.

As if someone, having taken up a desire for art or science, lest he should have a perfect knowledge of his education, says: 'Reveal to me what are the luminous things of science, so that I might know what I have and what I lack.' It is blessed to have things, works, and thoughts that are countable, those worthy of being numbered. Regarding the prostitute, it is indeed said: 'They are countless, whom you have slain' (Hosea 13:9). This does not necessarily mean that they are infinite, but that they are not worthy of being numbered. They do not exist in any word or number. So that I might know what I lack. If I learn the number of my days and my end, until when it is reached, I recognize in what things I lack, which are the things I have not yet learned. Therefore, those making a desire for science...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
